description: Small RNAs give cells a sequence-specific way to shut off messages that have already been made, tuning the output of hundreds of genes and enforcing the developmental and stress programmes that microRNAs control. An Argonaute protein loaded with a microRNA or siRNA guide scans mRNAs for complementarity; when the match is exact, AGO2, the only human Argonaute with endonuclease activity, slices the target, while imperfect pairing instead represses translation and speeds deadenylation and decay. AGO1, AGO3 and AGO4 lack cleavage activity and work only through this second route. The TNRC6 scaffolds bind Argonaute and recruit the deadenylase and decapping machinery that carries out the silencing, concentrating the complex in cytoplasmic foci. The same guide-directed recognition can also feed back on chromatin to silence transcription. Loss of this post-transcriptional silencing deregulates proliferation and differentiation, and Argonaute-microRNA circuits are broadly disturbed in cancer.

Only about half the ribosomal RNA gene copies in a nucleus are transcriptionally active at any time, and this pathway describes how ERCC6 (CSB) and the histone methyltransferase EHMT2 (G9a) keep that active fraction switched on, setting the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth. CSB is recruited through TTF1 bound at the Sal box terminator of rRNA repeats and brings in G9a, which dimethylates histone H3 lysine 9 across the transcribed region; CBX3 (HP1gamma) reads that mark and reinforces polymerase I output, a loop that persists only while transcription continues. The accompanying nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase components, including CHD3/CHD4, HDAC1/2, MTA and RBBP4/7 subunits, act on the same chromatin to shape rRNA gene state. Loss of CSB function deregulates polymerase I transcription and contributes to the growth failure and neurodegeneration of Cockayne syndrome.

Ribosome production is expensive, and cells keep only a fraction of their hundreds of rRNA gene copies transcriptionally active; the nucleolar remodeling complex is how the rest are shut down and kept that way. TIP5 (BAZ2A) partnered with the ATP-dependent remodeller SNF2H repositions the promoter nucleosome into a silent configuration, guided to rDNA by a promoter-associated noncoding RNA bound through its TAM domain and by an interaction with transcription termination factor TTF-I at a promoter-proximal site. Recruitment of SIN3-associated HDAC1 and HDAC2 removes histone acetylation, and DNMT1 and DNMT3B together with the methyl-CpG reader MBD2 impose heritable CpG methylation, locking copies off across cell divisions. The silenced state opposes the RNA polymerase I machinery and its SL1/UBTF initiation factors listed here, setting rRNA output, nucleolar organisation and genomic stability of the repeat array; loss of this restraint accompanies unchecked growth in cancer.

Long double-stranded RNA, whether from a virus or from transcribed repeats and transposons in the genome, is converted here into the short guides that silence matching transcripts. siRNA biogenesis is the entry point of RNA interference, giving cells a sequence-specific way to suppress parasitic nucleic acids and providing the basis for experimental and therapeutic gene knockdown. DICER1 cleaves the duplex into 21-25 nucleotide products while bound to TARBP2 or PRKRA within a RISC-loading complex, and the duplex is handed to an Argonaute protein; of the four human Argonautes, AGO2 is the one with slicer activity and is found largely on the cytosolic face of the rough endoplasmic reticulum as well as in the nucleus. The passenger strand is discarded, and the translin-associated nuclease pair TSN and TSNAX contributes to processing the discarded RNA.

Ribosome production begins with transcription of the rRNA genes by RNA polymerase I, and before that polymerase can be loaded the nucleosomal rDNA promoter must be made accessible. This opening step sets how many rRNA genes are active, and therefore the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth, which is why it is tuned to nutrient and proliferative signals and is deranged in cancer and in ribosomopathies. The upstream binding factor UBTF binds and bends promoter DNA, displacing histones to create a nucleosome-free region; its phosphorylation, with MAPK3 among the kinases implicated, governs productive engagement with the polymerase I initiation complex. Core histones of all four classes represent the chromatin being remodelled, while MBD2 and PHF6 act on the repressive side, keeping a fraction of rDNA repeats silent. The output is an initiation-competent promoter rather than any metabolic product.

Ribosome production begins with transcription of the rRNA genes, and RNA polymerase I transcription initiation is the step that sets how many ribosomes a cell will build — a rate that scales directly with growth, and one that is raised in proliferating and tumour cells. At the rDNA promoter the selectivity factor SL1, built from TBP with the Pol I-specific TAF1A–TAF1D subunits, forms a platform together with the architectural activator UBTF; phosphorylation of UBTF and the adaptor RRN3 then license loading of the multisubunit polymerase, whose POLR1 catalytic core shares several small subunits with Pol II and Pol III. Initiation output is tuned by reversible acetylation of the basal machinery through the KAT2A/KAT2B acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC1/HDAC2 within NuRD-type chromatin remodelling complexes, while the terminator-binding factor TTF1 links promoter events to rDNA chromatin state and nucleolar organisation.

Cytosine methylation is the chemical mark that lets a cell keep a stable record of which genes it should not express, and it is copied to daughter cells at each division. Three active methyltransferases transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine to cytosine, mostly in CG dinucleotides: DNMT1 acts on hemimethylated sites generated by replication and so maintains existing patterns, while DNMT3A and DNMT3B, aided by the catalytically inactive DNMT3L, place new marks during the genome-wide remethylation that follows early embryonic and germline erasure. UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated DNA and modified histones and recruits DNMT1 to replicating chromatin, which explains why core histones accompany the enzymes here and links methylation to histone marks. Methylated promoters and CG islands are silenced, supporting imprinting, X inactivation and repression of repeats; aberrant patterns and DNMT3A mutations are recurrent in cancer and overgrowth syndromes.

Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 lays down the initiating mark of heritable gene silencing, trimethylating lysine 27 of histone H3 to keep developmental regulators off in cells where they do not belong. This is how lineage decisions are made stable and inherited through division; its loss or hyperactivity underlies developmental syndromes and cancers, and gain-of-function EZH2 mutations drive lymphoma. The catalytic subunit EZH1 or EZH2 works only within a core containing EED and SUZ12, with RBBP4/RBBP7 and accessory factors such as JARID2, AEBP2, MTF2 and the PHF1/PHF19 Polycomb-like proteins shaping recruitment to CpG-rich, unmethylated promoters; EZHIP restrains catalysis. The resulting H3K27me3 is read by PRC1, which ubiquitinates H2A and locks in repression. PRC2 also associates with DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B, linking histone methylation to CpG DNA methylation and longer-term epigenetic memory.

Roughly half the human genome is retroelement-derived, and keeping those sequences transcriptionally silent is the job of the KRAB zinc finger protein family, the largest group of transcription regulators encoded by our genome. Each KRAB-ZFP uses its zinc finger array to recognise a particular class of transposable element, and the family has expanded in step with retroelement invasion, an evolutionary arms race in which younger elements are bound by fewer factors. Silencing is executed through the scaffold TRIM28, which binds the KRAB domain, is SUMOylated via UBE2I and SUMO2, and recruits effectors: the histone H3K9 trimethyltransferase SETDB1 with its partner ATF7IP, heterochromatin protein HP1, and the NuRD deacetylase complex built on HDAC1/2, MTA and CHD3/4 subunits. The resulting heterochromatin protects genome stability, especially in early embryos and germ cells, and its loss permits retrotransposition, aberrant transcription and innate immune activation.

Germ cells must keep transposons from mobilising in the genome they pass to the next generation, and piRNA biogenesis supplies the small RNAs that enforce that silence. Long precursor transcripts are made by RNA polymerase II from piRNA clusters, individual transposons and intergenic regions, then processed without Dicer: the mitochondrial phospholipase D PLD6 generates mature 5' ends, an exonuclease trims the 3' end, and HENMT1 adds a 2'-O-methyl mark that stabilises the 26-30 nucleotide product. Loaded PIWI proteins split the labour, with PIWIL1 and PIWIL2 acting in cytoplasmic cleavage and a ping-pong amplification loop, while PIWIL4 with TDRD9 enters the nucleus to direct DNA methylation of target loci. Tudor-domain partners, the helicase MOV10L1, MAEL and chaperone activity organise these complexes in germ granules. Loss of the pathway derepresses L1 elements and arrests spermatogenesis, causing male infertility.

Active removal of DNA methylation lets cells erase an epigenetic mark rather than wait for it to be diluted by replication, and it is how imprints are erased in primordial germ cells and how the paternal genome is demethylated in the zygote. The TET dioxygenases oxidize 5-methylcytosine stepwise to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine; thymine DNA glycosylase then excises the formyl- and carboxyl-modified bases, leaving an abasic site that base excision repair restores to unmodified cytosine. The oxidized intermediates are themselves abundant marks in embryonic stem cells and neurons, where TET1 expression tracks neuronal activity, while TET3 acts in oocytes and zygotes. TET2 predominates in haematopoietic stem cells and behaves as a tumour suppressor, its loss-of-function mutations being recurrent in myeloid malignancy. The pathway thus links chromatin state, developmental reprogramming and DNA repair chemistry.

WDR5 is a scaffolding hub that nucleates chromatin-modifying assemblies, and this pathway covers how those complexes are built. WDR5 joins RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 to form the WRAD module that licenses and positions the six KMT2 methyltransferases (KMT2A-D, SETD1A, SETD1B), which deposit mono-, di- and trimethylation on histone H3 lysine 4 at active promoters and enhancers. Complex-specific partners diversify targeting: MEN1 and the protease TASP1 with KMT2A/B, KDM6A, NCOA6, PAXIP1 and PAGR1 with KMT2C/D, and CXXC1 with WDR82 in the SET1 complexes. WDR5 also sits in the GCN5/PCAF-ATAC and KAT8-NSL acetyltransferase complexes, linking H3K4 methylation to histone acetylation. This machinery sets Hox gene expression during embryonic patterning and lineage specification; germline loss causes chromatinopathies such as Kabuki and Wiedemann-Steiner syndromes, and KMT2A rearrangement drives mixed lineage leukemia, making the WDR5 interface a drug target.

Ribosome production is the cell's largest biosynthetic commitment, so rRNA transcription must track nutrient supply; SIRT1 provides that link by negatively regulating rRNA expression when energy is scarce. Acting as an NAD-dependent histone deacetylase, SIRT1 senses a high NAD/NADH ratio during glucose limitation and, together with nucleomethylin (RRP8) and the H3K9 methyltransferase SUV39H1, forms a nucleolar silencing complex that deacetylates and dimethylates histone H3 on ribosomal DNA chromatin. Recognition of pre-existing H3K9me2 by the complex allows the repressive mark to spread across adjacent nucleosomes, closing the rDNA repeats to the RNA polymerase I machinery represented here by TBP and the SL1 subunits TAF1A-TAF1D. The result is coordinated restraint of ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation under metabolic stress, a form of energy-dependent nucleolar silencing linked to caloric restriction responses, nucleolar stress signalling and cellular ageing.

MicroRNAs are short RNAs that tune the output of most human genes, and their biogenesis is the multi-step route from a transcribed hairpin to a loaded silencing complex. The pathway sets how strongly hundreds of mRNAs are translated and degraded, shaping differentiation, proliferation and stress responses; loss of the processing machinery is embryonically lethal, and its disruption is a recurrent feature of tumours. RNA polymerase II generates a primary transcript whose hairpin is cropped in the nucleus by DROSHA with its partner DGCR8, exported by Exportin-5 in a Ran-GTP-dependent step, and cut by DICER1 with TARBP2 or PRKRA to a short duplex. One strand is discarded and the guide strand is retained by an Argonaute protein, of which AGO2 alone can slice highly complementary targets, forming the effector complex that directs post-transcriptional silencing.

RNA polymerase III makes the short, abundant, untranslated RNAs a cell needs constantly dash tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others dash and chain elongation is the productive phase in which the enzyme, having opened its promoter and escaped initiation, processively extends the transcript to its termination signal. Because tRNA and 5S rRNA supply are set here, the output of this polymerase scales with ribosome production and growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and other neurodevelopmental disease, while activating lesions raise its output in cancer. The sixteen-subunit enzyme is built from a catalytic core of the largest and second-largest subunits together with subunits shared with the other nuclear polymerases, plus a Pol III-specific subcomplex that handles promoter opening and RNA cleavage. Alternative forms of one subunit distinguish enzyme variants with differing gene preferences and a role in cytosolic DNA sensing.

Ribosome production depends on a steady supply of 5S ribosomal RNA, and this is the route by which RNA polymerase III is loaded onto the 5S rRNA gene, the classic type 1 promoter with its internal control region. Assembly is strictly ordered: the nine-zinc-finger factor TFIIIA binds the internal promoter first, creating a platform for the multisubunit TFIIIC complex, which in turn positions a TBP-containing TFIIIB built around BRF1 and BDP1 upstream of the start site; TFIIIB then recruits the polymerase itself, whose catalytic core (POLR3A, POLR3B) is completed by subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Output from this pathway sets the ceiling on ribosome assembly and is tied to growth control, and mutations in polymerase III subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and impair innate sensing of cytosolic DNA.

Ribosome production begins with RNA polymerase I making a single long precursor rRNA in the nucleolus, and transcription of that gene must be stopped cleanly at the end of the repeat so the polymerase can be recycled and the transcript released. In this termination step the DNA-binding factor TTF1 occupies a terminator element downstream of the rRNA gene and stalls the elongating enzyme; the release factor PTRF/CAVIN1 then acts on the paused complex to free both the nascent pre-rRNA and polymerase I from the template. The gene set accordingly includes the full polymerase I catalytic core and its shared subunits, the SL1 promoter-selectivity complex with TBP and the TAF1 proteins, the nucleolar activator UBTF, and TFIIH components that couple this transcription to repair. Output here sets the ceiling on ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation.

Retrotransposons and integrated retroviral DNA are transcriptionally silenced by the Human Silencing Hub, a three-subunit complex of MPP8, Periphilin and TASOR that keeps young LINE-1 elements, some HIV proviruses and other intronless foreign sequences switched off. This surveillance protects genome stability and limits insertional mutagenesis, and it is also why therapeutic transgenes and viral vectors are often epigenetically shut down. Recognition works partly through nascent transcripts bound by Periphilin and partly by reading existing H3K9 trimethylation, after which the methyltransferase SETDB1 with its partner ATF7IP, together with EHMT1/EHMT2, marks surrounding nucleosomes; the chromatin remodeller MORC2 compacts the locus. Components of the nuclear RNA exosome targeting complex, including MTREX, ZCCHC8 and RBM7, link the silenced transcripts to degradation. Long exons of host genes are sensitive, while introns confer protection, making transcript architecture the discriminating signal for self versus non-self DNA.

Ribosome production sets the pace of cell growth, and this chromatin-remodelling route raises output by opening the rDNA repeats so that RNA polymerase I can transcribe them efficiently. The B-WICH assembly, built around the ATP-dependent remodeller SMARCA5 with BAZ1B, nuclear myosin MYO1C, actin, DDX21, DEK, MYBBP1A, ERCC6 and SF3B1, binds active ribosomal RNA genes and also the polymerase III-transcribed 5S rRNA and 7SL RNA genes. By sliding nucleosomes and recruiting histone acetyltransferases such as EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, it converts the surrounding histones to an acetylated, transcriptionally permissive state that favours loading of the SL1 promoter-selectivity factor (TAF1A-TAF1D with TBP) and the Pol I catalytic core. The result is coordinate control of rRNA and signal recognition particle RNA synthesis, linking nucleolar activity to growth signals, with GSK3B among the kinases modulating the response.

RNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs in bulk tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others and this step ends each round of synthesis, freeing the transcript and the DNA template so the enzyme can recycle onto a new gene. Termination is driven almost entirely by the polymerase itself: a run of thymidines on the non-template strand is enough to destabilise the elongation complex, without the dedicated release factors or extensive cis-elements that other polymerases require. The seventeen-subunit enzyme is represented here in full, including subunits shared with polymerases I and II and the alternative catalytic-region paralogues POLR3G and POLR3GL. Released nascent transcripts bearing 3' oligo-U are captured by the La protein SSB, which protects them from exonucleolytic trimming and guides folding and maturation. Output from this machinery sets the ceiling on translational capacity and cell growth.

Transfer RNAs are not only adaptors for translation; they are also substrates for regulated cleavage that yields tRNA-derived small RNAs, and this biogenesis route is how cells convert a stress signal into a new class of regulatory RNA. Longer tRNA halves arise from a single cut in or near the anticodon loop, while shorter fragments come from cleavage closer to the 5' or 3' end, and 3' trailers left over from precursor maturation persist as their own species. Among the ribonucleases implicated are the secreted, endocytosed angiogenin, which cuts the anticodon loop under starvation and other stresses, the double-strand-specific DICER1, and ELAC2, which releases 3' trailers from particular tRNA precursors. Production is induced by hypoxia, oxidative stress, nutrient deprivation, hormones and viral infection, linking tRNA metabolism to translational repression, stress granule formation and gene silencing.

RNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs constantly — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others — so the rate at which it commits to productive synthesis sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and ribosome production. This step describes what happens immediately after the enzyme opens promoter DNA: the polymerase repeatedly synthesises and releases very short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent transcript, before it escapes the promoter and elongates processively. Promoter recognition upstream of this depends on distinct assembly factors for the different promoter classes — the multisubunit TFIIIC complex with TFIIIA at 5S genes, TBP-associated BRF1 and BDP1 at tRNA genes, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex and ZNF143 at U6-type type 3 promoters. The La protein binds the uridylate-rich 3' ends of the released products. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies oncogenic growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.

A handful of small non-coding RNAs, notably the spliceosomal U6 snRNA, are made by RNA polymerase III from gene-external promoters that look more like those of polymerase II genes than like classical tRNA promoters. Initiation from these metazoan-specific type 3 promoters supplies the U6 and related transcripts on which pre-mRNA splicing and other RNA processing depend, so the cell's capacity to mature its own messages is set here. Recognition begins at the proximal sequence element by the five-subunit SNAPc complex (SNAPC1-SNAPC5), which cooperates with the polymerase III-specific TFIIIB variant built on BRF2, BDP1 and TBP bound at a TATA box; together they load the seventeen-subunit polymerase, whose core shares several small subunits with polymerases I and II. Upstream enhancer elements add POU2F1 at an octamer motif and the zinc-finger factor ZNF143 at the SPH element to raise output.

Fat cells are made by a transcriptional programme in which the nuclear receptor pair PPARG and RXRA, once bound by lipid ligands, switches on the genes of lipid uptake, storage and droplet formation. Here that switch is coupled to chromatin: the related histone H3K4 methyltransferases KMT2C and KMT2D, with their shared complex subunits ASH2L, RBBP5, WDR5, DPY30, PAXIP1, PAGR1, NCOA6 and the H3K27 demethylase KDM6A, are recruited to PPARG:RXRA sites and deposit activating marks, while Mediator, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators are exchanged for NCOR1/NCOR2-HDAC3 corepressors. The output genes define the adipocyte — adiponectin, FABP4, CD36, perilipins, LPL, DGAT2, SCD, PNPLA2 and LIPE — and also drive thermogenic brown fat and hepatocyte triglyceride synthesis. Loss of the methyltransferase activity blocks adipogenesis and protects against diet-induced hepatic steatosis, the first step toward fatty liver disease, steatohepatitis and cirrhosis.

Small RNAs are best known for silencing messenger RNAs in the cytoplasm, but the same machinery also works in the nucleus, where it can switch target genes on or off at the level of transcription itself. Argonaute proteins loaded with microRNAs are carried across the nuclear envelope by importin-8 and by RAN-dependent import of the shuttling scaffold TNRC6A, then engage chromatin and RNA polymerase II at loci whose sequences match the guide RNA. The outcome depends on the chromatin marks recruited: DNA cytosine methylation with histone H3 lysine-9 and lysine-27 methylation accompany transcriptional gene silencing, whereas H3 lysine-4 methylation accompanies RNA activation, which is why core histones and the full polymerase II complex accompany the Argonautes here. Nuclear small RNAs have additionally been linked to alternative splicing choices and to the response to DNA double-strand breaks, extending guide-RNA specificity into genome maintenance.

Transfer RNAs and other short non-coding RNAs are made by RNA polymerase III, and type 2 promoters are the internal A-box/B-box arrangement found in tRNA and Alu-type genes. Initiation here begins with the multisubunit TFIIIC complex binding the two internal boxes directly, without needing the TFIIIA zinc-finger factor required at 5S rRNA promoters. TFIIIC then recruits TFIIIB, built from BRF1, BDP1 and TBP, which positions the polymerase over the start site; once TFIIIB is stably engaged, it alone can sustain repeated rounds of transcription. The seventeen-subunit enzyme includes catalytic POLR3A and POLR3B plus subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Output from this system sets the cell's translational capacity, is tuned to growth and nutrient signals through mTOR and MYC, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and related neurodevelopmental disease.

Ribosome production begins with rRNA transcription, and promoter escape by RNA polymerase I is the step where an assembled initiation complex commits to processive synthesis. Cells tune this step to match ribosome supply to growth demand, so it sits at the heart of nucleolar function and of growth control; its dysregulation accompanies rapid proliferation in cancer and underlies ribosomopathies. The polymerase I catalytic core with its specific subunits engages rDNA through the SL1 complex of TBP and TAF1A/TAF1B/TAF1C together with the activator UBTF, and the initiation factor RRN3 dissociates as the enzyme clears the promoter and enters elongation, unlike polymerase II initiation there is no requirement for ATP-driven promoter melting. Shared small polymerase subunits, TFIIH components including CDK7-cyclin H and the helicases ERCC2/ERCC3, chromatin-bound histones and PHF6 provide the nucleolar chromatin context in which escape occurs.

Transposable elements are a standing threat to germline genome integrity, and piRNA-guided silencing of endogenous retroelements is how germ cells keep them quiet across generations. Short PIWI-interacting RNAs, generated from transposon and non-coding transcripts and amplified by successive rounds of cleavage, load onto PIWI proteins and find their targets by base-pairing with nascent or mature transcripts, triggering either co-transcriptional or post-transcriptional repression. In the transcriptional arm represented here, PIWIL4 engages nascent retroelement RNA and, through SPOCD1 and C19orf84, recruits de novo DNA methylation machinery including DNMT3A and its cofactor DNMT3L, together with nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase activity and BAF-type chromatin remodellers acting on the surrounding histones. This imprinting of methylation during the perinatal window of germ cell reprogramming establishes lasting retroelement repression; its loss derails spermatogenesis, and SPOCD1 mutations cause male infertility.
